title: Visceral leishmaniasis in two brothers; diagnostic dilemma due to hemophagocytic syndrome
case_text:
An 8 year-old boy from Tehran (younger brother) presented with prolonged fever, abdominal pain and jaundice since 2 months ago. He had history of travel to an endemic area for VL in a province located in north of Iran 4 months ago. He had been previously hospitalized for 14 days and he had been monitored in the intensive care unit; however, no cause could be ascertained for his fever. He was then referred to our center. At the time of admission, the child was febrile, with toxic appearance and marked jaundice. On physical examination he had hepatosplenomegaly. His kidney function tests and respiratory and cardiovascular systems were normal.
Laboratory tests at the time of admission revealed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 5.4, WBC < 1000, PLT 63,000). The patient had deranged liver function (serum bilirubin 2.4 mg%, AST 152,000, ALT 147,000, LDH 601, ALK-P 1443). Blood and urine cultures were sterile and peripheral smear was negative for malaria parasite. The patient was also found to be negative for antibodies to HIV, hepatitis A, B, C, D virus, CMV, EBV, Borrelia and malaria. Ultrasonography of the abdomen revealed diffuse hepatosplenomegaly without any focal lesion. CT scan of abdomen revealed hepatosplenomegaly with para-aortic lymphadenopathy and pleural effusion. Laboratory findings included pancytopenia, hyperlipidaemia, elevated levels of ferritin and LDH. Bone marrow Aspiration (BMA) was performed three times. All of them were negative but his brother had a positive BMA for Leishman Donovan bodies and numerous histiocytes showing hemophagocytosis. With the final diagnosis of HPS associated with VL, The child was treated with glucantime/cyclosporine and corticosteroids. His condition was cured following treatment.
Unfortunately after one year of treatment two brothers expired due to HPS relapse.

You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Leishmaniasis
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: visceral leishmaniasis associated with hemophagocytic syndrome
